# Open Stacks

> A research wiki on exploring the world's literature cheaply and well: what is free and legal (open-access books and papers, public domain), cheap and institutional access routes (subscriptions, public and university libraries), discovery and AI research tools, reading environments from e-ink to VR, the legal constraints on building tools, a reference architecture for a personal catalog of everything, and a gallery of interface mockups and prototypes. Maintained by QURI (quantifieduncertainty.org) as part of the CAIRN project. Every page is a dated working draft; prices and product statuses are as of October 2026.

The organizing idea: separate the catalog (titles, tables of contents, summaries, topic placement: small, mostly open data) from the content (scattered across open repositories, libraries, subscriptions and paywalls), then build one place to browse everything that routes each work to wherever it can actually be read, at the right page. Sibling wikis: Robust Reasoning Processes (https://reasoning-processes.quantifieduncertainty.org) and Evaluation Engineering (https://evaluation-engineering.quantifieduncertainty.org).


## Start Here

- 1. Open Stacks (planned) — planned, not yet written
- [2. What to Do First](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/start-here/decision-guide/): A priority-ordered plan for a Bay Area researcher who wants to browse and read thousands of books, textbooks and papers cheaply and legally, with the time, cash cost and evidence for each step as of October 2026. Free routines and library cards come first, then papers, free textbooks, subscriptions (usually none), searching inside books, AI research tools, a returnable VR test, and what to build with Claude Code.
- 3. Cruxes (planned) — planned, not yet written

## Part I — Getting the Text

- [4. Open-Access Books and Textbooks](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/open-books/): How much of a technical researcher's reading list exists as a free, legal book (24 of 55 canonical titles in a test; 8 of 10 in ML, none of six 1930–1989 classics), what DOAB, OAPEN, OpenStax, LibreTexts, the Open Textbook Library and author-hosted PDFs actually contain as of October 2026, and an ordered routine for finding the free copy.
- [5. The Public Domain and Open Corpora](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/public-domain/): What is in the US public domain as of October 2026 (everything published before 1931, plus unrenewed US books to 1963), how Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, Wikisource, HathiTrust, the Internet Archive and LibriVox differ for a technical reader, why Internet Archive rights flags cannot be trusted, which licence-clean corpora (Common Pile, Common Corpus, Institutional Books) are usable building material, and what pre-1931 books are good for.
- [6. Open Papers and Preprints](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/open-papers/): How much of the journal literature is legally free (about half of recent articles, about a third of cited pre-2001 work), where the free copies live, the 2025–2026 policy and OpenAlex pricing changes that matter, and an ordered legal workflow for getting any paper, with hit rates recomputed from the best recent coverage study.
- 7. Grey Literature and Community Archives (planned) — planned, not yet written
- [8. Cheap Subscriptions](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/subscriptions/): What an individual can buy without an institution as of October 2026 (O'Reilly, Perlego, Everand, Kindle Unlimited, Kobo Plus, Springer+, JPASS, DeepDyve and used books), with catalog composition, a 53-title coverage spot-check, the AI-use clauses that bind tool builders, which subscription (if any) suits which reader, and a one-hour test against your own reading list.
- [9. Public Libraries](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/public-libraries/): What a free San Francisco Public Library card unlocks (O'Reilly, Libby, LinkedIn Learning, article databases, newspapers), what each extra Bay Area card and an LAPL card add for technical and for humanities reading, which out-of-area routes are closing, and how Link+ and interlibrary loan cover print-only books. Eligibility, holdings and prices as of October 2026.
- [10. University and Employer Access](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/academic-and-employer/): What an unaffiliated Bay Area researcher can get from UC Berkeley, Stanford and SF State libraries as of October 2026, and what each route costs once eligibility is priced in (remote access needs an Extension course or a visiting-scholar appointment). Also covers what employer licenses from O'Reilly, JSTOR, Springer Nature and Elsevier forbid, especially AI processing.
- 11. Your Own Library (planned) — planned, not yet written
- [12. The Shadow Libraries](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/shadow-libraries/): Sci-Hub, Library Genesis, Z-Library and Anna's Archive as of October 2026 — their measured coverage against legal routes, the lawsuits and blocking orders against them, their role in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta, and the legal risks to readers and tool builders. Shows where the legal access gaps actually are and why Open Stacks routes only to legal sources.
- [13. The Access Ladder](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/access/access-ladder/): Every legal route to a book or paper, ordered from free to expensive (open and author copies, public domain, Open Library lending, public library cards, walk-in academic access, cheap subscriptions, UC Berkeley Extension or visiting-scholar status, buying), with each rung's cost, setup time, coverage on small spot-check samples, license limits and indexability as of October 2026. Includes a 30-book worked example, a cost-against-coverage table, and the minimal-cost bundle for a Bay Area researcher.

## Part II — Finding Things

- [14. Catalogs and Metadata](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/finding/catalogs-and-metadata/): The open and paid bibliographic metadata available to anyone building a catalog in October 2026 (Open Library, WorldCat, Library of Congress, HathiTrust, Wikidata, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, DOAB/OAPEN, Google Books, ISBNdb, LibraryThing, Open Syllabus), compared on size, fields, licence, rate limits and bulk access. Also covers why work/edition clustering is the main engineering cost, where tables of contents and descriptions can be found, what a catalog built from metadata alone can do, and the legal facts about Anna's Archive metadata.
- [15. Browsing the Stacks](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/finding/browsing-the-stacks/): Why shelf browsing works (borrowing data show a 9- to 22-fold neighbour effect), what Library of Congress shelf order gives a reader and what it scatters, what happened to virtual shelf browsers from Harvard's StackLife to Open Library Explorer, and how to build a digital stacks browser with multiple placements, semantic "wormholes", access badges and LLM-assisted reclassification.
- [16. Searching Inside Books You Don’t Have](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/finding/searching-inside-books/): Page-level search for in-copyright books you cannot read, as of October 2026. Covers what HathiTrust, Internet Archive and Open Library, Google Books, Amazon, HTRC Extracted Features and the Ngram Viewer each return; a workflow, run live, that finds which books discuss proper scoring rules and on which pages; and how to turn the hits into a borrow, buy or subscribe plan.
- [17. AI Research Assistants](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/finding/ai-research-assistants/): The October 2026 landscape of AI tools for finding, synthesizing, browsing and reading scholarly literature, organized by job and priced; what independent audits show about their recall and citation accuracy; why books are missing; a recommended stack; and a Claude Code + web search + Zotero MCP baseline for building your own.
- [18. Curation: Syllabi, Experts and Reviews](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/finding/curation/): How to choose what to read in a new field using syllabi (Open Syllabus), expert lists (Five Books, public bookshelves), great-books canons and long-form reviews (ACX, LessWrong); what the evidence says about recommenders versus curation; a four-hour method for building a field's reading list; and guards against LLM-invented books.
- 19. Lectures, Talks and Podcasts (planned) — planned, not yet written

## Part III — Interfaces: What Has Been Tried

- [20. Foraging and Exploratory Search](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/interfaces/exploratory-search/): The theory and evidence on how people explore large information spaces (information foraging, berrypicking, the sensemaking loop, Shneiderman's mantra, exploratory search) and the interfaces built on it (Scatter/Gather, faceted search, fisheye views, TileBars, overview+detail), with what cheap LLM metadata now unblocks and twelve design principles for a literature explorer.
- [21. Maps of Knowledge](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/interfaces/maps-of-knowledge/): What science maps, citation-graph tools, embedding maps and topic models can and cannot do for a reader, from the evidence on whether maps help people find relevant work and why 3D information spaces failed. Ends with a costed specification, with its limits, for a 2D map of a personal 10,000-book catalog.
- [22. Reading Interfaces](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/interfaces/reading-interfaces/): What research prototypes and products show about reading at different depths (Ai2's Semantic Reader prototypes, LiquidText, MarginNote, explorable explanations, Distill, the mnemonic medium, Gwern.net's popups, StretchText and semantic zoom, and the skimming literature), with study results, costs at October 2026 prices, and which ideas carry over from papers to books.
- [23. Generative Interfaces](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/interfaces/generative-interfaces/): What the evidence says about generating pages, interfaces and study material on the fly for research reading, from Google's Generative UI study, the MCP Apps and A2UI standards, generated encyclopedias (STORM, Grokipedia) and Wikipedia's ban on LLM-written articles, and the Learn Your Way RCT to measured citation, book-summary and long-context error rates. Includes October 2026 costs and latencies, a split between what to curate, precompute and generate, and a claim-level provenance design.

## Part IV — Where You Read

- [24. Reading Modes and Devices](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/environments/reading-modes-and-devices/): Reading at four depths (survey, lookup, deep study, review) and what the evidence says about each, including Adler's inspectional and syntopical reading, skimming and speed reading, the screen-vs-paper meta-analyses (where dedicated e-readers did no better than tablets), listening vs reading, and spaced repetition. Also covers annotation workflows, a device table (e-ink, iPad mini, monitors, text-to-speech) with October 2026 prices, formats, library-app support and PDF legibility, and a graded matrix of modes against methods, tools and devices.
- [25. VR and Spatial Computing](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/environments/vr-and-spatial-computing/): Headsets and display glasses as a place to read and work, as of October 2026. Compares the hardware on price, weight, pixels per degree, passthrough and Mac support, reviews the desktop-streaming software and the evidence on legibility, reading speed, week-long VR work and eye strain, and ends with who should try it and a two-week self-experiment for deciding.
- [26. Building a Virtual Reading Room](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/environments/virtual-reading-room/): What it takes, as of October 2026, to build your own spatial reading room (from a 360° skybox to a WebXR library to a native app), which platforms let a custom room sit behind other apps' windows, and a build plan for a WebXR library in LC call-number order over Open Library data. The room is cheap; legible text and your desktop are the hard parts, and the spatial-memory evidence favours stable 2.5D placement over 3D.

## Part V — Building Your Own

- [27. The Legal Map](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/building/legal-map/): What a builder of literature tools may store, summarize, search, cache, scrape and link as of October 2026, rated green, yellow or red separately for a personal tool and a public service, with the cases, TDM exceptions, license terms and API terms behind each rating. US focus, with EU, UK and Japan notes; not legal advice.
- [28. A Reference Architecture](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/building/reference-architecture/): A buildable design for a personal "catalog of everything" built from bulk-first source adapters, an immutable raw lake, ID crosswalks and work clustering, a unified work record, a best-free-copy resolver, parsing, enrichment, static-first indexes and several UIs. Includes October 2026 data sizes, rate limits, parser benchmarks, embedding and index options, build tiers and the failure modes that sink such builds.
- [29. Costs and Effort](https://open-stacks.quantifieduncertainty.org/building/costs-and-effort/): What a personal "catalog of everything" costs in money and hours as of October 2026. LLM enrichment at 1k, 100k and 10M works, embeddings, storage, static vs server hosting, Claude Code effort tiers, where costs blow up, a worked example with the arithmetic, and when building beats buying subscriptions.
- 30. The Design Space (planned) — planned, not yet written
- 31. Prototype Gallery (planned) — planned, not yet written
